veranderings.rede: With 'het', the standard order puts the object before 'gaan' plus the infinitive.

veranderings.voor: Jy roep 'n grootmens en jy koel die brandwond op dieselfde tyd
veranderings.na: Jy roep 'n grootmens, en jy koel die brandwond terselfdertyd
veranderings.rede: 'Op dieselfde tyd' calques 'at the same time' (Afrikaans: 'terselfdertyd'), and AWS requires a comma before 'en' joining two clauses with their own subject and verb.

veranderings.voor: Toe het sy nie gestaan en wag nie
veranderings.na: Toe het sy nie staan en wag nie
veranderings.rede: After 'het' the 'staan en' construction takes the bare form, as the lesson itself does with 'het sit en lees'; 'gestaan en wag' mixes the two forms.

veranderings.voor: Die water bly nou twintig minute lank aan en ek hou die tyd
veranderings.na: Die water bly nou twintig minute lank loop, en ek hou die tyd dop
veranderings.rede: 'Die water bly aan' and 'ek hou die tyd' are English calques ('stays on', 'keep time'); 'bly loop' matches the lesson's later wording, and the clause comma follows AWS.

veranderings.voor: net die brandwond moet koel word
veranderings.na: net die brandwond moet afgekoel word
veranderings.rede: 'Koel word' means 'become cool'; the passive 'be cooled' needs the participle 'afgekoel word'.

veranderings.voor: om sy skouers en sy lyf toegedraai
veranderings.na: om sy skouers en sy lyf gedraai
veranderings.rede: With 'om' the natural verb is 'draai' (as the lesson says of the plastic later); 'toegedraai' doubles the idea of wrapping.

veranderings.voor: Die kraan het bly loop en die res
veranderings.na: Die kraan het bly loop, en die res
veranderings.rede: AWS comma before 'en' joining two clauses that each have their own subject and verb.
'Ná' with the accent marks 'after' and avoids reading it as the preposition 'na' (to).
'Ná' with the accent marks 'after', consistent with the earlier time phrase.
'Die middag' is vague in a past-tense story; 'Daardie middag' clearly points to the afternoon of that same day.
A comma after the embedded relative clause stops two verbs running together and helps a Grade 6 reader.
Fingers are 'opgesteek' in Afrikaans; 'opgehou' usually reads as 'stopped'.
